passage: I'm Tejas. When I joined the city coaching centre from our small-town school, the physics sir said on day one, "Students from small-town boards usually struggle with our level. Don't take it personally." I did take it personally. Before each weekly test my neck went stiff before the paper even landed. I rushed, then went back and changed answers I'd been sure of. My scores sat near the bottom. But in the evenings, solving the same problems with Hrithik at the tea stall, I got most of them right, fast. Hrithik noticed first. "You're only bad when sir's watching." It was true. The tests weren't measuring what I knew. They were measuring how afraid I was of proving sir right.

qa.a: Sir may see the low scores as proof of weak ability, missing that the fast, correct evening work shows the real level and the pressure causes the drop.

grounding: A teenager from a small-town school, told such students struggle, grows tense in tests, rushes and changes right answers, so scores reflect pressure, not ability.

passage: Mentor's note, school coding club, 12 February. Written by Bhupen Sir. Alka, fifteen, is one of two girls in the club and among my strongest. In practice she solves the hardest problems calmly. At Saturday's inter-school contest, a boy from another team said loudly, "Girls' team? Easy round, then." I watched Alka's shoulders rise. She typed fast, submitted without testing, and got two answers wrong that she had solved in practice last week. She kept glancing at the scoreboard as if it were judging her personally. The result says she is weak; her practice sheets say otherwise. On Monday I showed her both side by side and told her the contest measured pressure, not skill. Next time we will practise under timed, noisy conditions, and I will ask the organisers to deal with remarks like that one.

qa.a: He showed Alka her practice sheets beside the contest result, so she could see the drop came from pressure, not lack of skill.

qa.q: What would change if the organisers dealt with remarks like the boy's?
qa.a: Girls in the contest could focus on the problems instead of on proving someone wrong, so results would reflect their real ability.

grounding: A mentor records how a strong girl coder, hearing a remark about girls, rushes and doubts known answers in a contest, so her result looks like low ability.

passage:
Tuesday night
Chemistry unit test today. I knew the whole equilibrium chapter. Did it on the bus with Noor yesterday and got every question.
But Mrs Kulkarni said, handing out papers, "Sports quota students, just attempt what you can." She wasn't even being mean. Half the class turned to look at me and Vivek, the two boys from the hockey team.
After that my hands went cold. I rushed the first page in ten minutes so no one could say I was slow. Then I changed two right answers to wrong ones because they suddenly looked too easy for someone like me. Left the last question blank.
Got 14 out of 30. Noor saw it and said, "That's not you. You explained the whole chapter to me."
Maybe it isn't me. Maybe it's the looking.
Tushar

qa.q: What did Mrs Kulkarni say while handing out the papers?
qa.a: She said, 'Sports quota students, just attempt what you can.'

qa.q: Why did Tushar change two right answers to wrong ones?
qa.a: He started doubting himself under the label, feeling the answers looked too easy for someone like him.

qa.q: What could Tushar try before the next test to ease the pressure?
qa.a: He could remind himself that he knew the chapter on the bus, and slow down on the first page instead of rushing to prove he isn't slow.

qa.q: How does Noor see Tushar's 14 out of 30?
qa.a: Noor sees it as not reflecting him at all, because Tushar was the one who explained the whole chapter to Noor.

grounding: A sports-quota teenager expected to do poorly grows tense in a chemistry test, rushes and doubts known answers, so the result hides real ability.
